sentences.text: The name Barbaridactylus combines a reference to the Barbary Coast of North Africa with the Greek word for "finger".
The type specimen of Barbaridactylus (FSAC-OB 232) includes a right femur, left radius, ulna, humerus, scapulocoracoid, and a partial mandible.
Four additional specimens referred to Barbaridactylus consist entirely of humeri.
Barbaridactylus possessed upward-curving jaws, a trait shared with other nyctosaurids.
The fused scapulocoracoid in Barbaridactylus suggests that the animal was likely an adult.
Barbaridactylus had a long, thin humeral shaft and a hatchet-shaped deltopectoral crest located distally, resembling that of Nyctosaurus more than Alcione.
The ulna of Barbaridactylus is relatively gracile with weakly expanded ends, contrasting with the robust ulna of Alcione.
The femur of Barbaridactylus expands gently rather than showing the strong distal expansion seen in other nyctosaurids, resembling the femur of Pteranodon.
Barbaridactylus was first described in 2018 by Nicholas R. Longrich, David M. Martill, and Brian Andres.
All known specimens of Barbaridactylus were found during a three-year excavation that recovered approximately 200 pterosaur fossils.
Only one fossil occurrence of Barbaridactylus has been recorded.
The ecosystem where Barbaridactylus lived included sharks, bony fish, turtles, plesiosaurs, and mosasaurs.
Recent studies indicate that at least five other pterosaur species, including Alcione, Simurghia, and Tethydraco, lived alongside Barbaridactylus at this location.
Barbaridactylus belongs to the family Nyctosauridae.
Barbaridactylus is classified as a reptile.
The type species of the genus Barbaridactylus is Barbaridactylus grandis.
Barbaridactylus lived in the Ouled Abdoun Basin of Morocco during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Barbaridactylus fossils were found in upper Maastrichtian phosphates in the Ouled Abdoun Basin of Northern Morocco.
The layer containing Barbaridactylus dates to the latest Maastrichtian, approximately 1 million years before the end-Cretaceous extinction event.
Barbaridactylus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
Phylogenetic analysis originally placed Barbaridactylus as the sister taxon of Nyctosaurus lamegoi within the family Nyctosauridae.
Brian Andres suggested in 2022 that Barbaridactylus might actually be an additional species of Nyctosaurus.
A 2024 analysis recovered Barbaridactylus outside the genus Nyctosaurus as the sister taxon of Muzquiopteryx, while reclassifying Nyctosaurus lamegoi as a species of Simurghia.
